**Choose the smaller linear system when dimensions are very unequal.** Ordinary ridge solves for d feature coefficients. When d is huge but there are only n examples, the same solution can be expressed through n example weights instead. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html) [3](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/)

The identity $(X^TX+\lambda I)X^T=X^T(XX^T+\lambda I)$ lets the inverse move across X transpose in the appropriate way. Solve $(XX^T+\lambda I)\alpha=y$, then recover $w=X^T\alpha$.

**An illustrative size comparison.** With 1000 examples and 100,000 features, a dense d-by-d matrix has ten billion entries, while the n-by-n Gram matrix has one million. Building either still involves data processing, but the factorization and storage difference is substantial.

Kernel ridge replaces inner products with a kernel and predicts from similarities to training examples without explicit feature weights. Sparsity and iterative solvers can change which route is best. The primal and dual formulas are mathematically equivalent under the stated penalty; neither requires explicitly computing an inverse. Consider serving cost too, because a kernel prediction may depend on many training examples.

**Technical details and references.**

The identity $(X^TX+\lambda I_d)X^T=X^T(XX^T+\lambda I_n)$ implies $(X^TX+\lambda I_d)^{-1}X^T=X^T(XX^T+\lambda I_n)^{-1}$ for $\lambda>0$, the same result obtained from Woodbury. Therefore solve $(XX^T+\lambda I_n)\alpha=y$ and set $w=X^T\alpha$. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html) [3](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/)

Dense primal construction/factorization costs roughly $O(nd^2+d^3)$ and $O(d^2)$ memory; the dual costs $O(n^2d+n^3)$ and $O(n^2)$ memory. Thus the dual is attractive when $d\gg n$, though sparsity and iterative solvers can change the comparison. Kernel ridge replaces $XX^T$ by $K$, predicting $k(x,X)^T\alpha$ without explicitly constructing feature weights. The formula is an algebraic equivalence, not a requirement to compute either inverse explicitly.
